checklists.title: Leaving a building during an alarm

steps.title: Treat the alarm as real
details: Treat every alarm as real until it is officially confirmed otherwise.
Nobody can tell from the sound alone whether an alarm is a drill, a fault or a real fire.
A message from a colleague, a rumour or the alarm falling silent is not official confirmation.

steps.title: Stop and take only what you carry
details: Stop non-essential tasks. Take only what you can carry in a few seconds; never delay your exit to collect belongings.
Never go back for an item, even if it is only a few metres away.

steps.title: Use the stairs, not the elevator
details: Do not use elevators during a fire. Use the stairs.
On the stairs, walk at a steady pace and hold the handrail. Do not run, push or stop on the landings.

steps.title: Check a closed door first
details: Before opening a closed door, feel it with the back of your hand. If it is hot, do not open it. Use another route.
If the door is cool, open it slowly and be ready to close it at once if you see smoke or feel heat.

steps.title: Move through smoke
details: Smoke and hot gases rise. Stay low, where the air is cleaner, and cover your nose and mouth with cloth if possible.
Keep one hand on the wall to hold your direction and move to the nearest safe exit.
Close doors behind you. This slows the spread of fire and smoke.

steps.title: Go to the assembly point
details: Go to the designated assembly point, away from the building and its entrances so responders have access.
Report to the person responsible for the headcount. Report anyone missing and their last known location.
Do not re-enter the building until it is declared safe by responders.

steps.title: Check the scene is safe
details: Check that the scene is safe first. Do not become a second casualty.
Check responsiveness (speak to the person and gently tap the shoulders), then breathing (look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds).
Deal with life-threatening problems first: not breathing and severe bleeding.

steps.title: Call for help
details: Call 112 or the local emergency number. Give the location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards. Stay on the line until told to hang up.
Assign one specific person to call, for example: "You, call 112 and tell me what they said."

steps.title: Press on the wound
details: Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing, and keep the pressure on.

steps.title: Add layers, do not remove
details: If the cloth soaks through, add more layers on top instead of removing it.
If a limb wound bleeds heavily and pressure does not control it, a tourniquet may be applied by someone trained and equipped. Note the time.

steps.title: Keep the person lying down and warm
details: Keep the person lying down and warm, and monitor them until help arrives.

steps.title: Hand over to responders
details: Give a short, ordered handover: what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since.
Name any missing person and the last place they were seen.

steps.title: Deal with life threats first
details: Deal with life-threatening problems first: not breathing and severe bleeding.
Check that the scene is safe first. Do not become a second casualty.

steps.title: Cool the burn
details: Cool the burn under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes.

steps.title: Do not apply anything else
details: Do not apply ice, butter, oils or toothpaste.
Do not burst blisters.

steps.title: Cover the burn loosely
details: Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing.

steps.title: Know when to seek medical help
details: Seek medical help for large or deep burns, burns on the face, hands or genitals, or if you are unsure.
